Consult Summary:
- Acute diarrheal illness (most consistent with acute viral gastroenteritis) in the context of brief 3-day course with dehydration not evident; SSRIs may contribute to GI symptoms; management provided focuses on hydration, diet modification, and symptom monitoring.

History:
- Presenting complaint: 3 days of diarrhea with intermittent abdominal pain and a single episode of vomiting; patient otherwise tolerating fluids.
- Timeline: Symptoms began about three days ago; progressed to four to five bowel movements per day; no clear improvement yet.
- Symptom details: Stool described as watery/loose, with variable consistence (time of day effects noted); no blood or mucus detected.
- Associated symptoms: Mild appetite reduction; able to drink and maintain fluid intake; no significant fever documented (mild fever at most described); no orthostatic symptoms or severe system involvement.
- Exposures: No recent travel or notable dietary exposures reported; no known contact with ill individuals noted.
- Alarming symptoms: No hematochezia, no high fever, no signs of severe dehydration reported at presentation.
- Pertinent negatives: No blood in stool; no mucus in stool; still able to drink fluids; no travel exposures; no overt dehydration.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (current condition acknowledged by patient).
- Other medical history not clearly documented in the visit notes.
- Family history notable for father with hypertension and death from bowel cancer at age 62.
- Allergies: None reported.

Medications:
- Lexapro (escitalopram) reported by patient; intended as inhaler in conversation but likely a miscommunication on the visit. Dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Asthma inhaler: patient indicated use but specific inhaler name not confirmed in the notes; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: None documented.

Social History:
- Location: London.
- No tobacco use or alcohol/drug use details provided.
- No travel or exposures reported beyond local context.

Family History:
- Father with hypertension.
- Father died of bowel cancer at age 62.
- No other familial cancers or GI conditions documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Not recorded.
- General/appearance: Patient described as well-appearing and not dehydrated during the visit.
- Abdominal/GI exam: Not recorded in detail in the transcript.
- Hydration status: Clinician noted adequate hydration status at presentation.

Investigations:
- No laboratory tests or imaging were ordered during this visit.
- No stool studies were obtained at this time; discussion included criteria to obtain stool testing if symptoms persist or worsen.

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
- Working diagnosis: Acute diarrheal illness most consistent with acute viral gastroenteritis given (~3-day) onset, 4–5 loose stools per day, absence of blood, patient’s ability to maintain hydration, and no travel/exposure history. Alternative considerations include acute bacterial gastroenteritis and SSRI-induced diarrhea; colorectal cancer is unlikely in this context but acknowledged due to family history.

DDx Integration (top items with supporting/opposing notes):
- Acute viral gastroenteritis
  - Supporting: Onset ~3 days; 4–5 watery stools/day; abdominal pain; one vomiting episode; no blood; patient able to maintain fluids.
  - Opposing: No explicit sick contacts; only mild fever described.
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis
  - Supporting: Diarrhea with abdominal pain; relatively acute presentation.
  - Opposing: No travel/exposure history; no fever or systemic toxicity described.
- SSRI-induced diarrhea (Lexapro)
  - Supporting: Lexapro use present; diarrhea is a known SSRI side effect.
  - Opposing: No clear temporal linkage between starting Lexapro and symptom onset; infectious etiologies remain plausible.
- Note: No evidence supporting inflammatory bowel disease or colorectal cancer as likely causes given the current history and age; but family history of bowel cancer was acknowledged to maintain awareness of red flags.

Issue 1: Acute diarrheal illness (likely viral gastroenteritis)
- Diagnosis/Impression: Acute viral gastroenteritis suspected; patient is hemodynamically stable and not dehydrated at presentation.
- Plan:
  - Hydration: Encourage continued oral hydration; assess for dehydration; provide guidance on adequate fluid intake.
  - Diet: Implement a soft diet during diarrhea (crackers, toast, jam) with gradual reintroduction of more regular foods as tolerated.
  - Foods to avoid during illness: dairy, heavy/fatty meats, eggs initially; reintroduce meats after 48 hours of symptom improvement.
  - Gut flora/restoration: Consider probiotic-containing foods (e.g., yogurt) to support gut flora.
  - Over-the-counter support: Dioralyte (electrolyte solution) recommended as needed to replenish salts and fluids.
  - Monitoring and red flags: If diarrhea persists beyond 7 days, or if stool becomes bloody, obtain stool sample; if diarrhea worsens to 6–8 stools/day or signs of dehydration develop, seek urgent care or hospital assessment.
  - Follow-up: Review notes in the patient app; return for reassessment if symptoms worsen or do not improve within 1 week.

Issue 2: SSRI-associated diarrhea (Lexapro)
- Diagnosis/Impression: Possible contributor to GI symptoms given Lexapro use.
- Plan:
  - Pharmacologic adjustment: No immediate changes implemented; encourage discussion with prescribing clinician if symptoms persist or worsen; monitor for temporal relationship with medication changes.
  - Counseling: Educate patient on potential GI side effects of SSRIs and when to seek medical advice.

Issue 3: Family history and cancer risk considerations
- Diagnosis/Impression: Family history notable for bowel cancer; current presentation not highly suggestive of colorectal pathology, but red flags to monitor.
- Plan:
  - Red-flag education: Advise patient to seek evaluation if new blood in stool, unintentional weight loss, persistent abdominal pain, or persistent diarrhea beyond 1 week or with systemic symptoms.
  - No immediate stool testing unless symptoms persist or red flags arise; consider stool testing if symptoms persist beyond 1 week or if blood appears.

General Plan and Follow-Up:
- Education: Provided guidance on hydration, soft diet, probiotic foods, and use of Dioralyte; explained the plan and when to seek urgent care.
- Documentation: All guidance and instructions to be accessible via patient app notes.
- Follow-up: Reassess in 1 week or sooner if red flags develop (blood in stool, dehydration, worsening diarrhea, fever, or inability to maintain hydration).

Quality Checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: Vitals not recorded; comprehensive physical exam not documented; medication reconciliation incomplete due to inconsistent medication naming in the transcript.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None identified; DDx aligned with the clinical presentation described in the transcript.
- Transcript quality: Some conversational inconsistencies (e.g., Lexapro described as an inhaler), but overall sufficient to determine working diagnosis and management plan.

Document Quality Summary:
- Allergies: None documented.
- Medications reconciliation: Lexapro listed with dose/route/frequency not documented; asthma inhaler name not confirmed; consider clarifying in future visits.
- Exam/vitals: Not fully recorded; observational note of hydration status provided.

End of note.
